c037.front: What happens when a NOT IN list contains NULL?
c037.back: The query returns no rows. x NOT IN (1, NULL) is never TRUE, because a comparison with NULL gives UNKNOWN. Use NOT EXISTS or filter the NULLs out in the subquery (WHERE ... IS NOT NULL).

c038.front: > ALL and > ANY when the subquery returns no rows?
c038.back: > ALL (empty set) is TRUE for every row: there is nothing to "lose" against. > ANY (empty set) is FALSE: there is nothing to "win" against, so 0 rows.
c038.try_sql:
-- Empty set: > ALL lets all 9 rows through, > ANY none
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees e WHERE e.salary > ALL (SELECT salary FROM employees WHERE 1 = 0)) AS all_cnt,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees e WHERE e.salary > ANY (SELECT salary FROM employees WHERE 1 = 0)) AS any_cnt
FROM dual;

c039.front: What do ANY and ALL correspond to?
c039.back: = ANY is the same as IN. <> ALL is the same as NOT IN. > ALL means: greater than the MAX. < ANY means: less than the MAX.

c040.front: A scalar subquery returns 0 rows, or 2 or more. What then?
c040.back: 0 rows → the result is NULL. 2 or more rows → error ORA-01427.

c041.back: A subquery that uses a column of the outer query, for example WHERE e2.department_id = e.department_id. Logically it is evaluated again for each row of the outer query.
c041.try_sql:
-- The subquery uses e.department_id: the average is computed for each employee's department
SELECT e.last_name, e.department_id, e.salary
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary > (SELECT AVG(e2.salary) FROM employees e2
                  WHERE e2.department_id = e.department_id);

c042.front: Where can you put a subquery?
c042.back: In the SELECT list (scalar), in FROM (an inline view), in WHERE and in HAVING. In DML: INSERT ... SELECT, UPDATE SET column = (subquery), and also as the target of a DML statement.
c042.try_sql:
-- Subqueries in SELECT (scalar), in FROM (inline view) and in WHERE
SELECT d.department_name,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees e WHERE e.department_id = d.department_id) AS cnt
FROM (SELECT department_id, department_name FROM departments) d
WHERE d.department_id IN (SELECT department_id FROM employees);

c400.front: A correlated UPDATE without WHERE: what about the rows for which the subquery finds nothing?
c400.back: They are changed too: they get NULL (or 0 when the subquery uses COUNT). To change only the matching rows, add WHERE EXISTS with the same correlation condition.

c401.front: Does a correlated UPDATE/DELETE see its own earlier changes in the subquery?
c401.back: No. Each run of the subquery sees the data as it was at the start of the statement (statement-level read consistency).

c402.front: How do you set two columns with one correlated subquery?
c402.back: UPDATE t a SET (a.c1, a.c2) = (SELECT b.x, b.y FROM s b WHERE b.id = a.id). The parentheses around the column list are required, and the number of columns must match (otherwise ORA-00947 or ORA-00913).

c403.front: Correlated DELETE: how do you delete rows that have no match in another table?
c403.back: DELETE FROM t a WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM s b WHERE b.id = a.id). NOT IN works only when the subquery returns no NULL.

c404.front: Can a subquery in WHERE have ORDER BY?
c404.back: No: you get ORA-00907 missing right parenthesis. ORDER BY is allowed in an inline view (in FROM) and at the end of the outer query.

c405.front: Which operators work with a subquery that returns many rows?
c405.back: IN, NOT IN, EXISTS, NOT EXISTS, and any comparison operator followed by ANY (SOME) or ALL, for example > ALL. The plain = < > LIKE BETWEEN need one row.

c1400.front: A scalar subquery in SELECT finds two rows for one outer row. What happens?
c1400.back: The whole query fails with ORA-01427. Oracle does not duplicate the row (a join does that) and does not pick one of the two. Only an empty result turns into NULL.
c1400.try_sql:
-- Departments 20 and 30 have several employees each: the whole query fails
SELECT d.department_name,
       (SELECT e.last_name FROM employees e WHERE e.department_id = d.department_id) AS emp
FROM departments d;

c1401.front: The WITH clause (subquery factoring): what can you do with a named query?
c1401.back: Use it several times in the main query (in FROM and in subqueries). A later named query in the same list can use it too: WITH a AS (...), b AS (SELECT ... FROM a).
c1401.try_sql:
-- avg_sal uses dept_sal, and the main query uses both
WITH dept_sal AS (SELECT department_id, SUM(salary) AS total
                  FROM employees GROUP BY department_id),
     avg_sal AS (SELECT AVG(total) AS avg_total FROM dept_sal)
SELECT d.department_id, d.total
FROM dept_sal d
WHERE d.total > (SELECT avg_total FROM avg_sal);

c1402.front: Inline view (SELECT order_id, SUM(qty) FROM ... GROUP BY order_id) v: can the outer query use v.total?
c1402.back: No: ORA-00904 "V"."TOTAL": invalid identifier. There is simply no such column. Give the expression an alias inside the view: SUM(qty) AS total.

c1403.front: Does DISTINCT in a subquery fix ORA-01427?
c1403.back: Only when one value remains. The programmers' salaries 9000, 6000, 4800 are still three rows. Use IN / = ANY, or an aggregate function if you really mean one value.

c1404.front: x NOT IN (a subquery without NULLs), and x itself is NULL?
c1404.back: The result is UNKNOWN, so the row does not come back. department_id NOT IN (20) skips Grant (department NULL): 5 rows, not 6.
c1404.try_sql:
-- Grant (department NULL) does not come back: 5 rows, not 6
SELECT last_name, department_id FROM employees
WHERE department_id NOT IN (SELECT department_id FROM departments
                            WHERE department_name = 'Sales');

c1405.back: "Different from at least one value". When the list has two different values, it is TRUE for every value that is not NULL. NOT IN is <> ALL, not <> ANY.

c1406.front: > ALL and > ANY when the subquery returns NULL next to other values?
c1406.back: > ALL: never TRUE (it is an AND with UNKNOWN), so 0 rows. > ANY: one TRUE is enough, so the NULL does not get in the way.
c1406.try_sql:
-- commission_pct has NULLs: > ALL gives 0 rows, > ANY all 9
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees e WHERE e.salary > ALL (SELECT commission_pct FROM employees)) AS all_cnt,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees e WHERE e.salary > ANY (SELECT commission_pct FROM employees)) AS any_cnt
FROM dual;

c1407.back: Pairwise: (a, b) IN (SELECT x, y ...): the pair must match together. Non-pairwise: a IN (...) AND b IN (...): each column is checked separately, so extra rows may come out ("crosswise" matches).

c1408.front: EXISTS with a subquery that does not refer to the outer query?
c1408.back: The result is the same for every row: all rows if the subquery finds anything, or none. Usually it is a sign that the correlation condition was forgotten.

c1409.front: SET (a, b) = (SELECT x ...) and SET (a) = (SELECT x, y ...): which errors?
c1409.back: Too few columns in the subquery: ORA-00947 not enough values. Too many: ORA-00913 too many values. Oracle does not fill the gaps with NULLs.
c1409.try_sql:
-- Two columns, one value: ORA-00947
UPDATE employees e
SET (e.salary, e.commission_pct) = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees)
WHERE e.employee_id = 108;

c1410.front: UPDATE ... SET col = (SELECT val ...) WHERE EXISTS (SELECT ...): can col still get NULL?
c1410.back: Yes. EXISTS only checks that a matching row exists, not that the value is not NULL (for example product 15 has list_price NULL). Add a val IS NOT NULL condition or use NVL.

c1411.front: A correlated DELETE should delete three rows, but one of them still has child rows. What happens?
c1411.back: Error ORA-02292 (child record found), and the whole statement is rolled back: nothing is deleted. Oracle does not skip the "troublesome" row.
